summary: A survey of New-Protocol Telnet servers from September 1974. It is a status snapshot updating RFC 701, and it is itself updated by RFC 669.

eli5.summary: This is the September 1974 progress check on which computers had finished the new Telnet.

questions: which telnet options were implemented in 1974
subtitle: A September 1974 headcount of which ARPANET hosts ran the new Telnet protocol and which options they supported.

tldr.problem: The network was moving from the old Telnet protocol to a new one, and people needed to know which server hosts had made the change.
tldr.mechanism: A surveying program run at various times, plus a few manual checks, tested each server from the new-protocol user Telnet at BBNA as of 23 September 1974 and tabulated the results.
tldr.outcome: Of 34 server hosts, 13 (38%) had a new-protocol server and 21 (62%) did not, so there was still a long way to go to 100% implementation.

today: RFC 702 is a point-in-time survey that updates RFC 701 and is updated by RFC 669, according to the unit metadata. Its figures describe September 1974 only.

sections.title: Changes Since Last Month
sections.content:
The previous survey produced a gratifying amount of feedback clarifying the status of several sites, but there were very few changes in the status of host servers. The report lists them in numerical order, with host numbers in octal.

UCLA-NMC is no longer a server, and host 205 is now BBN-TENEXD. SDC-LAB is temporarily off the list, I4-TENEXA (117) is not a server while KI4B-TENEX (217) is, and AMES-67 fixed a bug that revealed a new-protocol server with no options. ISI-DEVTENEX (226) and USC-ECL (327) were added.
sections.eli5: First comes a short list of who joined, who left and who fixed something since the last check.

sections.title: The Tally
sections.content:
The summary counts 34 total server hosts. Of these, 21 (62%) have no new-protocol server and 13 (38%) implement it. Within the 13, six hosts run the new protocol on socket 27 and the old one on socket 1, six run the new protocol on both socket 1 and socket 27, and one runs it on socket 1 only.

The six old-on-1, new-on-27 sites are the ones whose operation is 100% correct as the author understands the protocol and conventions. Some servers listed on socket 1 actually try to talk to both old and new user Telnets depending on the control sequences received. SU-AI appears to have a minor bug, sending an improper response to a request for option 0.
sections.eli5: About one in three computers had the new version ready and the rest were still on the old one. A few were mixed, and one had a small slip.

sections.title: Reading the Server Table
sections.content:
The tabulation lists each host number and name, its status on socket 1 and socket 27, and the new-protocol options implemented. X means no server at that socket, I# means option # is implemented incoming to the user (the server says WILL #), and O# means it is implemented outgoing from the user (the server says DO #).

The options implemented by anyone are 0 (TRANSMIT-BINARY), 1 (ECHO), 3 (SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD) and 6 (TIMING-MARK). Hosts such as BBN-TENEX list I1, 3, 6; O3, while AMES-67 and MIT-MULTICS list none.
sections.eli5: The table is a report card with a row per computer and a few letters and numbers telling which extra features each one knows.
